item.title: History of Underwear (Radio Edit)
item.content:encoded: Greg Jenner is joined in western Europe by historian Dr Serena Dyer and comedian and actor Vic Michaelis to learn all about the hidden history of underwear.For as long as people have been wearing clothes, they have been wearing garments under them – Romans at Hadrian’s Wall were sent underpants, and even Ötzi the Iceman was discovered wearing a form of undergarment. But what were people wearing before the invention of underwires and elastic, so essential to our modern conceptions of underwear?This episode traces the history of our underthings in western Europe and the USA from the medieval period, through the Tudor, Regency and Victorian eras, and into the modern day. Moving around the body, it takes in the linen shifts and shirts that were the universal undergarment for much of history, the development of drawers and stockings, and the shockingly recent invention of knickers and briefs. It also tackles stays and corsets, asking whether they were really as painful as film and TV depictions suggest, and looking at the reliability of on-screen underwear in programmes like ‘Bridgerton’.This is a radio edit of the original podcast episode. item.title: Lab-grown meat was supposed to save the world. What happened?
Temporal and Durable Execution for AI Agents
item.content:encoded: Coordinating long-running processes on top of distributed systems is one of the persistent hard problems in software. A process that runs across many steps can’t count on finishing in one clean pass, since the machines running it may crash, stall, or drop connections. To handle this fragility, developers have often resorted to writing layers of retries, timeouts, and checkpointing to keep state alive across failures. However, this custom plumbing is often brittle, hard to maintain, and can break down at scale.Temporal is an open-source platform built around an approach it calls durable execution. Developers write a workflow as a straightforward sequence of steps, and the platform preserves its full state underneath, so the code can survive a crash and resume exactly where it left off. The underlying technology was created at Uber over a decade ago. Since then, Temporal has become foundational infrastructure for AI and agent workloads, where long-running tools and agent loops need exactly this kind of durability.Maxim Fateev is a co-founder of Temporal. He returns to the show with Sean Falconer to discuss how durable execution works, why it’s infrastructure rather than a framework, how it fits the non-deterministic world of AI agents, its new capabilities, and why Temporal’s fully open source strategy is central to its moat.sponsor@softwareengineeringdaily.com

item.title: Body Snatchers: From the Grave to the Anatomy Table
item.content:encoded: Under the cover of darkness, body snatchers crept into graveyards across Georgian and Victorian Britain, digging up freshly buried corpses to sell to medical schools. Known as the Resurrection Men, they sparked widespread terror, forcing families to take extraordinary measures to protect their dead. But as demand for bodies grew, the trade took a sinister turn with the infamous murderers Burke and Hare.But were body snatchers a necessary evil in the advancement of modern medicine?Dan Snow is joined by Emma Sparre-Newman, Manager of London’s historic Brompton Cemetery, to uncover the macabre history of body snatching and its legacy.Produced by Mariana Des Forges and edited by Natasha Hughes and Dougal Patmore.Dan Snow's History Hit is a History Hit podcast.History Hit is part of Little Dot Studios, a Certified B Corp™.

item.title: 726. The Death of Captain Cook: Massacre on the Beach (Part 2)
Why More AI Usage Can Mean Lower Margins
item.author: Demetrios
item.content:encoded: In this episode, we’re joined by , Executive Director of the Tokenomics Foundation and the FinOps Foundation at the Linux Foundation, to dig into the question every AI-heavy company is now facing: you know what you’re spending, but can you prove what you’re getting for it?J.R. explains what tokenomics really means (and why it has nothing to do with crypto). The real cost of AI goes well beyond API tokens. It includes harnesses, idle compute, storage, data, and the people who build and run it all. We look at how companies like Canva have had to rethink pricing as AI usage eats into cost of goods sold, flipping the old idea that more engagement is always good news. J.R. also shares findings from a survey of around 500 large enterprises. Most were confident they could see their spend, but 75% couldn’t show value their CFO would defend.Along the way, we cover engineers caught building their next startup on the company’s AI budget, why spend caps can actually push teams toward better decisions, the gap between activity metrics like merged PRs and real business value, why CFOs avoid the term ROI, and how model routing can backfire by breaking your cache. We also get into why not every problem needs an LLM, and how power shortages at data centers are quietly pushing up the cost of AI for everyone downstream.[01:27] Meet J.R. and the Tokenomics Foundation[02:18] What tokenomics actually means[03:33] AI is rewriting pricing and margins[06:20] Rogue token spend and side projects[07:02] Internal AI vs product AI[09:04] Visibility first, then spend caps[09:39] Token spend vs merged PRs[10:29] Activity vs outcomes vs value[14:53] Why CFOs avoid saying ROI[15:51] Survey of 500 companies[17:30] Model routing and its hidden costs[18:27] Forecasting enterprise AI demand[21:34] Not everything needs an LLM[23:09] Power and the cost of AI

item.title: Steve Yegge on Building Software Factories
item.content:encoded: Building software with AI agents has moved beyond using a single assistant. A growing number of engineers are now running what they call software factories, teams of named, persistent agents that talk to each other, hold roles, and produce code around the clock. That shift surfaces a strange new set of problems, ones that are less about writing code and more about running an organization. The difficult questions become how to keep agents from over-constraining themselves into paralysis, how much autonomy to grant them, and how to introduce AI coworkers to the actual humans they end up messaging.Steve Yegge is a longtime engineer and writer, well known for his work at Google and Amazon and his influential writing on AI-assisted development. He has been building one of these factories at the far edge of what is currently possible, and he argues the primitives are starting to converge.In this episode, Steve returns to SED to speak with Kevin Ball about the rise of software factories, why treating agents like people saves tokens, the failures he has hit when agents lock themselves into rigid rules, agent project managers as a company’s first real AI employees, and his case that swarms of small models, not ever-larger frontier models, are where this is all heading.

The Berlin Airlift
item.content:encoded: In 1948, the ruins of Berlin became the first major battleground of the Cold War. Encircled behind the Iron Curtain, the German capital faced a brutal choice: submit to Stalin’s blockade, or freeze and starve. And with trigger-happy generals eyeing their atomic weapons, the Western Allies launched a humanitarian gamble that many condemned as utter madness.Dan Snow is joined by Joseph Pearson, author of 'The Airlift', to unpack the dramatic tale of the Berlin Airlift - from the story of an American pilot who once dropped bombs on Berlin, to that of a little girl who was upset that the older boys kept stealing her chocolate.Produced by James Hickmann and edited by Dougal Patmore.Dan Snow's History Hit is a History Hit podcast.History Hit is part of Little Dot Studios, a Certified B Corp™.

item.content:encoded: What is the greatest revolution in human history? Unlike the invention of the steam engine, the rise of states or the birth of modern industry, the answer HAS to be the moment humanity stopped hunting and gathering and started farming. item.title: Akhenaten and Nefertiti (Radio Edit)
item.content:encoded: Greg Jenner is joined in ancient Egypt by historian and curator Dr Campbell Price and comedian Sikisa to learn all about Tutankhamun’s parents, Nefertiti and Akhenaten.As well as their famous son, this ancient Egyptian power couple are best known in the modern age for two reasons. Firstly, Nefertiti’s legendary beauty – her portrait bust is instantly recognisable around the world. Secondly, Akhenaten’s religious radicalism, which saw him reorient Egyptian belief towards the sun god Aten and build an entirely new capital away from the traditional seat of power at Thebes.This episode traces their lives as members of the 18th dynasty, often regarded as the ‘Golden Age’ of pharaonic Egypt. We look at Akhenaten’s murky childhood and Nefertiti’s even murkier origins, exploring their family life and the children they had, the religious revolution that Akhenaten drove, the unique architecture and art styles developed during their reign, and the fate of Aten worship after Akhenaten’s death. Along the way, we dig into the archaeological evidence and the many uncertainties surrounding their lives, and ask whether they really were Tutankhamun’s parents after all.This is a radio edit of the original podcast episode. item.title: The Rise of the Software Factories
item.content:encoded: AI coding agents have made individual developers dramatically more productive, yet most organizations aren’t seeing anything close to that gain at the company level. A key reason is that shipping a feature to production involves far more than writing code. Triage, review, context, guardrails, and human approvals all surround the work, and agents add new risk by acting in ways teams can’t always see or control. Turning individual gains into real organizational throughput, has become one of the central challenges of the agentic era.Port is an AI software factory platform that lets platform engineers build, operate, and govern an AI software factory which is a layer that sits above the coding agents. The factory is model and agent agnostic while supplying a context lake that encodes an organization’s taxonomy and data, governance, and guardrails across each stage of the software lifecycle, human-in-the-loop checkpoints, orchestration across different agents, and a registry of approved agents and skills.Yonatan Boguslavski is the CTO and a co-founder at Port. In this episode, he joins Kevin Ball to talk about the shift from writing features to “factory engineering,” how a context lake structures organizational knowledge so agents can actually use it, how governance works across an agentic software lifecycle, and the build-versus-buy question of where a platform like Port fits.Full Disclosure: This episode is sponsored by Portsponsor@softwareengineeringdaily.com

item.title: Hatshepsut: Was This Really Egypt's Greatest Pharaoh?
item.content:encoded: What does it take to be a great ruler? Rameses II, Akhenaten, Seti I- the great Egyptian Pharaohs- would have you believe it's building towering monoliths and waging great wars. But shouldn't it be someone who maintains peace, manages diplomacy to create a flourishing and healthy civilisation?This is something the Pharaoh Hatshepsut was extraordinarily good at. In the 18th dynasty, she oversaw one of the most prosperous times in Ancient Egyptian history, expanded its influence further and made its people richer than ever before. Joining Dan to argue her case is Dr Campbell Price, curator of Egypt and Sudan at Manchester Museum.Produced by Mariana Des Forges and edited by Natasha Hughes and Dougal Patmore.Dan Snow's History Hit is a History Hit podcast.History Hit is part of Little Dot Studios, a Certified B Corp™.

item.title: From the archive: Dark waters: how the adventure of a lifetime turned to tragedy
The Technical Interview Is Broken
item.content:encoded: The technical interview has long been used as a proxy for actual job performance. Brain teasers, data structure puzzles, or reversing a linked list became the price of admission to employment as a developer in many organizations, even though few engineers do that work day to day. It would seem AI has now broken that model entirely, since an LLM can one-shot any classic algorithm question. This is forcing tech companies to rethink what an interview should measure.Vivek Ravisankar is the co-founder and CEO of HackerRank, which is one of the most well-known platforms for tech interview practice problems. In this episode, Vivek joins Josh Goldberg to discuss why old-style interviews stopped working, the company’s “apology tour” for years of algorithm puzzles, how to keep AI evaluation fair and trustworthy, and where both models and the shape of hiring may be headed as software engineering becomes something every role does.sponsor@softwareengineeringdaily.com

item.title: Multi-Cloud LLM Routing and Context-Aware Coding Agents
item.author: Demetrios
item.content:encoded: In this episode, we sit down with and , engineers at Cloudflare and Miro, to look at how two very different companies are building their own AI software factories, and what happens to engineering when the code mostly writes and reviews itself.We start with the AI gateway: why a model call is no longer simple when the same model is served across multiple regions, multiple clouds, and direct from the provider, and how Miro pools rate limits and data residency rules (like EU-only models for German customers) into a single routing layer that also powers Miro’s Sidekicks. Matt walks through Cloudflare’s agent stack, from the AI gateway and Agents SDK to Flue, a JavaScript agent framework from the makers of Astro, and Cloudflare OS, an open source agent office suite he even runs at home for grocery shopping.The heart of the conversation is code review. Matt describes what he calls the best AI code reviewer he’s ever used, built on Flue and powered by an internal engineering codex written only for agents. Scott breaks down Miro’s three-layer setup, including Easel, a bot that reads production logs overnight and opens fix PRs before anyone wakes up, and explains why only about half of those PRs get merged, and how that signal is fed back to teach the system what people care about.Along the way, we cover agent experience as a new discipline, how open source maintainers are handling a flood of cheap AI pull requests, Astro reaching zero open issues, when companies should open source internal tools and how to retire them gracefully, plus a few hot takes on chocolate and nuts. We close on the rise of the “scholarly engineer,” and why understanding ideas may matter more than reading every line of code.Timestamps:[00:00] Cold open[01:03] Meet Matt and Scott[01:20] What an AI gateway really is[02:28] Multi-region, multi-cloud model routing[05:00] Cloudflare’s agent stack and Cloudflare OS[06:43] The Flue framework from the Astro team[07:32] The best AI code reviewer[09:29] An engineering codex written for agents[11:48] Agent experience and evals[12:44] Miro’s Easel bot and three layers of review[15:55] Software factories and Astro hitting zero issues[18:58] Companies open sourcing internal tools[22:59] Hot takes[25:03] The scholarly engineer[28:50] Wrap up

item.title: Anne Bonny and Mary Read (Radio Edit)
item.content:encoded: Greg Jenner is joined in the 18th-century Caribbean by historian and curator Hannah Cusworth and comedian Kemah Bob to learn about the swashbuckling lives of pirates Anne Bonny and Mary Read. These women and their adventures on the high seas have become the stuff of legend, helped along by the sensational account of their lives written shortly after their capture.Though they are famous for the short period they spent together on a pirate ship, dressed as men to hide their true identities, the two had very different backgrounds. Anne was the well-off and rebellious daughter of a merchant and plantation owner in Carolina, while the working-class Mary already had experience dressing in men’s clothing and working as a sailor and soldier.This episode traces their biographies, exploring their upbringings, romantic entanglements (with men and each other), and time aboard the pirate ship captained by the infamous Captain 'Calico Jack' Rackham, as well as their ultimate fate. And it looks at the wider context of the Caribbean, the transatlantic trade in enslaved Africans and the Golden Age of piracy which shaped their lives and choices, and asks what place they have in queer and trans histories of the period.This is a radio edit of the original podcast episode. For the full-length version, please look further back in the feed.Hosted by: Greg Jenner Research by: Naomi Weaver Written by: Naomi Weaver, Dr Emmie Rose Price-Goodfellow, Dr Emma Nagouse, and Greg Jenner Produced by: Dr Emmie Rose Price-Goodfellow and Greg Jenner Audio Producer: Steve Hankey Production Coordinator: Gill Huggett Senior Producer: Dr Emma Nagouse Executive Editor: Philip Sellars

item.title: Why Stripe Cut 500,000 Internal Docs Down to 5,000?
item.author: Demetrios
item.content:encoded: What happens when AI agents start relying on the same messy docs your team already struggles to search?Demetrios hops into a Waymo in San Francisco with , founder and CEO of Falconer and co-author of Documentation for Developers. They talk about why developers and agents need different things from docs, why agents sometimes skip up-to-date instructions, and how a stale internal document can contribute to a production incident.Dave shares how Stripe cut roughly 500,000 internal docs down to 5,000 worth maintaining. The conversation also covers how to capture the reasoning behind engineering decisions, when a diagram beats a wall of text, and who owns the fallout when an agent acts on bad information.[00:00] Hopping into a Waymo in San Francisco[00:24] Meet Dave, founder of Falconer[01:15] Why internal docs matter for AI agents[03:24] What humans and agents each need from docs[05:46] Testing how well agents use developer tools[07:01] Why agents skip the latest docs[09:42] Decision records and the reasoning behind the code[14:04] Cleaning up stale docs and broken search[15:29] How Stripe went from 500,000 docs to 5,000[17:02] When a diagram beats a 10-page doc[18:53] How conflicting docs can lead to an incident[20:42] Who owns reliability when an agent makes a mistake?[24:01] Treating documentation as part of the product[26:38] Giving readers an escape hatch[27:27] The cost of AI-generated fluff[29:36] Wrap-up and post-show chat

item.title: Fraud Prevention in the Age of AI Agents
item.content:encoded: A major challenge for almost every online service is reliably identifying users, and knowing whether a given user or agent can be trusted. Historically, web services leaned on cookies stored in the browser to remember a visitor and recognize them when they return. The problem is that cookies live in the user’s own browser and are easy to remove, block, or avoid entirely, so a bad actor can simply clear them to escape recognition. IP blocking and CAPTCHA puzzles are firmer approaches, but they can frustrate legitimate users while doing little to stop a determined attacker. That leaves developers stuck between being too lax and losing control, or too strict and driving real users away.FingerprintJS was started in 2012 as an open-source project. In 2019, Fingerprint was launched as a separate, full commercial platform, built on the original FingerprintJS GitHub library, to recognize devices and browsers without relying on cookies. It handles identification by reading over 100 signals, from fonts and screen resolution to how a device renders audio and graphics.Keshia Rose works in Developer Relations at Fingerprint. In this episode she joins Gregor Vand to talk about fingerprinting, how Fingerprint combines multiple signals to identify fraudulent actors, how to distinguish legitimate AI agent use from anonymous or malicious bots, and how Fingerprint’s research team uncovered and disclosed a privacy vulnerability in Firefox and Tor that could have been used to track people across the web.Full Disclosure: This episode is sponsored by Fingerprint

item.title: GitLab and the Evolution of DevSecOps
item.content:encoded: AI coding agents can already reach well beyond the code in front of them. Through connections to tools like Slack, Jira, and Sentry, an agent can pull in issues, discussions, and production signals from across an organization. However, that context is scattered across many separate systems, with no shared map of how it all connects and no common controls over what an agent is allowed to touch. For a large enterprise, stitching that together while staying compliant, auditable, and sometimes fully cut off from the internet is a hard problem.GitLab runs one of the major platforms where software gets built, hosted, and shipped. That gives it a wide view of everything around the code, which shapes how it is approaching the agent era. The bet is that AI is most useful when it can draw on the full context of a project and stay under enterprise control, rather than acting as a point tool bolted onto a single repository. Getting there means wrestling with hard questions about governance, agent identity, and how much autonomy to hand over.Tim Zallmann is the VP of Engineering at GitLab. In this episode, he joins Gregor Vand to discuss bringing AI to the full software development lifecycle, why running agents under enterprise control matters for governance and auditing, how to track which human is behind an agent’s actions, the realities of shipping air-gapped software, and how the space is shifting as new players move into code hosting.

item.title: My AI Agent Bought Me A Car
item.author: Demetrios
item.content:encoded: ’s first real test of Hermes Agent was a shopping tool that matched clothes to photos of ancient pottery. A few months later, the same agent was checking government auction sites every day until it found him a retired three-wheel parking ticket car, which he now drives around San Francisco. In this episode, recorded at AGNTCon + MCPCon North America in San Jose, Sam, who works on the RL post-training team at Nous Research, goes from those everyday wins to the question everyone in AI is asking: can agents improve themselves?He explains how Hermes grew from an internal productivity tool into one of the most talked-about open-source agents, and why letting it write its own skills was the moment it clicked for users. He also describes an early version that could design its own RL environment, train on Thinking Machines’ Tinker, and hot-swap the new weights into a model running locally. Sam then breaks down Trace to Environment, an idea he credits to Xiaomi’s MiMo-V2.6-Pro work, and the loop Nous is building around it: find the exact point where an agent fails, cluster those failures by type, synthesize environments that recreate them, and train on them again and again.The second half moves from training to inference. We get into whether reasoning models overthink, why leaning on pretraining knowledge can be a model’s Achilles heel, and why choosing a reasoning effort level may be a temporary quirk. Sam also makes his case for activation steering as an underexplored way to get more out of small models, explains where steering meets interpretability, and describes what true continual learning could look like.Timestamps:[0:00] Cold open[1:21] Meet Sam from Nous Research[2:39] How Hermes Agent started[3:38] From pottery to a parking ticket car[7:40] Benchmarking life admin tasks[8:58] Agents that write their own skills[10:10] RL at Nous a year ago[12:24] Hot swapping self-trained weights[15:00] Xiaomi and Trace to Environment[17:22] Turning agent failures into training[20:27] Where the RSI conversation is heading[21:34] Token efficiency and overthinking[26:30] Steering models at inference time[32:35] Toward true continual learning[34:54] Wrap up

A Deep Dive on Submarines
item.content:encoded: For centuries, humans have been fascinated by the mysteries of the deep sea. The history of submarines is one of extraordinary invention, daring exploration and deadly warfare. From the first experimental underwater vessels of the 17th century to the devastating U-boats of the First and Second World Wars, submarines have transformed naval warfare and revolutionised our understanding of the oceans.Today, Dan visits the Royal Navy Submarine Museum in Gosport and is joined by curator Alexandra Geary to discover the eccentric origins of underwater travel and the dramatic submarine battles of WWI and WWII in honour of the 125th anniversary of the Royal Navy Submarine Service. He also speaks to Vice Admiral Sir Tim McClement, who was Second in Command on HMS Conqueror during the sinking of the Argentine ARA General Belgrano warship in the Falklands, as well as First Sea Lord General Sir Gwyn Jenkins on how AI might shape the submarines of the future.With huge thanks to Commander James 'Dally' Dalrymple and Annarose Hearsum.Produced by Mariana Des Forges, Beth Donaldson and edited by Dougal PatmoreDan Snow's History Hit is a History Hit podcast.History Hit is part of Little Dot Studios, a Certified B Corp™.
